food.text: As pineapple and sugarcane plantations grew, so did the demand for labor. Between 1850 and 1930, immigrant workers arrived in the Hawaiian Islands from China, Korea, Japan, the Philippines, Puerto Rico and Portugal, and each group brought its own cuisine.

In 1872 the Royal Hawaiian Hotel opened on Hotel Street, and it was one of the most refined hotels in the Pacific. Its dining room served dishes on par with the best restaurants in Europe, and an 1874 menu offered mullet, spring lamb, chicken with tomatoes, and cabinet pudding.

ʻOtai is a refreshing Polynesian drink, and European colonists documented the Samoan version in the late 19th century. The original recipe mixed grated ambarella fruit (vi in Samoan and Tongan) with young coconut meat, coconut milk and coconut water. It was poured into large coconut shells, corked with coconut husk, and chilled in cold water or waterfalls.

New dishes arrived with the immigrant workers in Hawaii. Chinese Cantonese char siu bao (manapua), Portuguese sweet bread and malasadas, Puerto Rican pasteles, and the Japanese bento all joined the existing indigenous, European and American foods.

Marin is credited with the first Hawaiian vineyard in 1815, where he planted the now rare Mission grape variety. Captain Vancouver had introduced grape vines around 1792. Marin also brewed the first beer in the islands in 1812.

Chinese immigrants brought Cantonese cuisine to Hawaii, cooking the first stir fry, sweet and sour, and dim sum dishes in the islands, served with rice. Rice cultivation was often done by reusing wet taro patches (loʻi).

Filipinos reached Hawaii in 1909, bringing peas and beans and the adobo style of vinegar and garlic dishes. They chose to boil, stew, broil and fry food instead of baking. They also ate sweet potatoes as a staple besides rice.

Marin, whom Hawaiians called "Manini", experimented with planting oranges, limes, beans, cabbages, potatoes, peaches, melons, maize and lettuce. He also planted the first coffee crop in 1817, but those plantings failed.
Chinese rice growers in Hawaii imported familiar fish varieties from Asia. They used them to stock local streams and irrigation ditches.

art.text: Many early European ships carried professional artists to record their discoveries. They sketched and painted Hawaii's people and landscapes using imported materials and concepts. Night scenes of erupting volcanoes were especially popular, giving rise to The Volcano School.

Christian missionaries first arrived in Polynesia in the 1790s. Hymns were instituted and native musical genres were driven underground and prohibited. Traditional polyphonic singing soon merged with church styles, and along with brass bands became an important part of Polynesian music culture.

In the 19th century, depopulation from slave raiding and Western diseases disrupted many Polynesian societies and cultures. Missionary work brought conversion to Christianity and sometimes the destruction of traditional artistic heritage, specifically sculpture. More secular forms, such as carving kava bowls and making tapa, continued.

Papeete Cathedral, dedicated to Our Lady of the Immaculate Conception, opened in 1875 near the waterfront of Papeete in Tahiti. It is the oldest Catholic church in Tahiti and one of Papeete's last remaining examples of early colonial architecture.

Hawaiian art made after Cook's arrival includes work by native-born and long-term residents that used western materials and ideas, such as paintings on canvas and quilts. Traditional arts such as kapa barkcloth also continued to be produced after Cook arrived in 1778.
Hawaii's influential kī hōʻalu, or slack key, music incorporated the Spanish guitar introduced in the late 19th century. It later introduced the steel guitar to country music.

Polynesian works of art were thought to contain spiritual power, or mana, and could effect change in the world. The collections of European explorers show that classical Polynesian art was still flourishing when they visited. The most famous Polynesian art forms are the Moai statues of Rapa Nui.
Inside Papeete Cathedral, a full-size woodcarving of the Madonna and Child mixes European and Polynesian features. The child is clutching a breadfruit. The work originated from the Marquesas Islands.

Papeete Cathedral is known for its Stations of the Cross, created by Yuel Durnad and St. Fond. The scenes mix Tahitian and Roman styles of dress, yet solely depict Polynesian people in The Passion. The paintings' style was influenced by Paul Gauguin.

Some of the first westerners to visit Hawaii were artists, who sketched and painted its people and landscapes using imported materials and concepts. Night scenes of erupting volcanoes were especially popular. They gave rise to what became known as The Volcano School.

The Kingdom of Tahiti was declared a French protectorate in 1842, and French missionaries began arriving that same year. An apostolic vicariate was established on May 9, 1848. Construction of Papeete Cathedral most likely started after this, and it was completed in 1875.

war.text: In 1844 the French and the Tahitians went to war on the island of Tahiti, a conflict that lasted until 1847. The technologically inferior Tahitians were no match for French marines in the field. At the Battle of Mahaena on 17 April 1844, 441 French soldiers defeated an under-equipped native force twice their size, and 15 French soldiers and 102 Tahitians died. After that defeat the Tahitians relied on their knowledge of the mountainous interior to wage guerrilla warfare from fortified valleys.

When Kamehameha I died in 1819, he left his son Liholiho a large arsenal, with tens of thousands of soldiers and many warships. The Hawaiian army and navy mixed traditional canoes and loincloths with Western cannons, muskets, ships and military ranks.

On 22 September 1914, the German armoured cruisers Scharnhorst and Gneisenau entered the port of Papeete on Tahiti and shelled the town and its fortifications. They finished off the French gunboat Zélée and the freighter Walküre, which the French had already begun to scuttle. The shelling set the town on fire, and two entire blocks of Papeete burned to the ground. A Japanese civilian and a Polynesian boy were killed by the German shellfire, though there were no military casualties on either side.

The Hawaiian Kingdom was overthrown in a coup on January 17, 1893, against Queen Liliʻuokalani. It began when the revolutionist John Good shot Leialoha, a native policeman trying to stop a wagon carrying weapons to the Committee of Safety. The Committee then organized armed non-native men and gave the Queen an ultimatum: give up her power, or have her subjects face violence at the hands of the Committee and the militia. Because there was no Hawaiian army, the Committee asked American minister John L. Stevens for U.S. Marines, and he sent Marines and sailors, who never fired a shot. Although the overthrow is often called bloodless, the Queen's Book says J.S. Walker lost his life from the treatment he received at the hands of the insurgents.

On 12 November 1815, Pōmare II won a decisive battle at Feʻi Pī against Opuhara, chief of the powerful Teva clan. The victory made him king of Tahiti and united the island under one family for the first time, ending Tahitian feudalism and the military aristocracy.

The Tahitian guerrilla campaign ended with the defeat of the Tahitians at the Battle of Punaruu in May 1846 and the capture of Fort Fautaua on 17 December 1846. In February 1847 Queen Pōmare IV returned from exile and agreed to rule under the French protectorate.

France also tried to conquer and annex the three neighboring island kingdoms in the Leeward Islands. In 1846 the warriors of Queen Teriitaria II of Huahine "massacred" the French forces at the Battle of Maeva, killing 18 French marines and wounding 43. The Jarnac Convention of 1847 then had France and Great Britain agree to respect the independence of Queen Pōmare's allies in the Leeward Islands.

Papeete had only a garrison of 25 colonial infantry and 20 gendarmes in 1914. Lieutenant Maxime Destremau moved the guns of the gunboat Zélée ashore, and several Ford trucks were turned into impromptu armored cars by mounting them with Zélée's 37 mm guns.

Stevens landed a company of US Marines from the USS Boston and two companies of sailors on January 16, 1893. The royal military and police forces made no effort to interfere, stop the revolution, or protect the Queen.

The Papeete raid had major strategic consequences. It disclosed the German cruisers' positions to the British Admiralty, which led to the Battle of Coronel. The depletion of Scharnhorst's and Gneisenau's ammunition at Papeete also contributed to their later destruction at the Battle of the Falklands.

literature.text: Missionary Robert Henry Codrington traveled widely in Melanesia and published several studies of its language and culture. His 1891 book The Melanesians: Studies in their Anthropology and Folk-Lore contains the first detailed description of mana in English.

In the 19th century, scholars compared mana to concepts they thought similar, such as the orenda of the Iroquois. They theorized that mana was a universal phenomenon that explained the origin of religions. Later scholarship and Indigenous communities view these theories as inaccurate.

In The Melanesians (1891), Robert Henry Codrington defined mana as "a force altogether distinct from physical power, which acts in all kinds of ways for good and evil." He added that it is of the greatest advantage to possess or control. This was the first detailed English description of the idea.

A notebook titled "Collected songs and legends from the southern Cook Islands (c. 1883–1912)" by John Joseph Knight Hutchin preserves written-down island material. Notebook 2 includes a tale titled E Tuatua no te apai atinga ki mua i te marae, meaning "Tale of the offerings at the marae in heathen time."

science.text: In 1880, the botanist and missionary William Colenso listed 48 varieties of kūmara, or sweet potato, grown in Northland, Hawke's Bay and the East Coast of New Zealand. They came in red, purple and white, in different shapes, and with rough or smooth textures.

The kioea was a large Hawaiian honeyeater, about 33 cm long, with a long, slightly curved bill and a broad black stripe on its face. It went extinct around the mid-19th century, leaving only four specimens in museums.

European and American explorers, traders and whalers arriving in the Hawaiian Kingdom introduced diseases such as syphilis, tuberculosis, smallpox and measles. The article calls these a disastrous series of imported plagues. The Native Hawaiian population fell from approximately 128,000 in 1778 to 71,000 in 1853, and reached a low of 24,000 in 1920. Kauikeaouli (Kamehameha III) witnessed cataclysmic losses of his people through imported diseases.
In New Zealand, the replacement of traditional sweet potato cultivars began in the early 19th century. Hardier and larger varieties from the Americas gradually took their place.

The cause of the kioea's extinction is mostly attributed to logging of its rainforest habitat, hunting, and the introduction of predators such as feral cats, dogs and pigs. The bird seems to have been in decline even before Europeans first arrived on Hawaiʻi.

Queen Emma of Hawaii, queen from 1856 to 1863 as the wife of King Kamehameha IV, was later known as a humanitarian. Native Hawaiians were in decline because of foreign-borne diseases like smallpox, so she encouraged her husband to establish a public hospital. In 1859 she established Queen's Hospital and visited patients there almost daily whenever she was in Honolulu.

Kūmara does not seed in New Zealand because of the climate. Mutations in buds, together with careful cultivation by growers, likely produced the many new varieties that William Colenso later recorded.
All four known kioea specimens come from the island of Hawaiʻi. Native Hawaiians seem to have been unfamiliar with the bird, and its feathers were not used in Hawaiian featherwork.

Northland Māori told William Colenso that a red-fleshed, red-skinned variety called paikaraka was the oldest kūmara variety, while Te Arawa sources in the 1940s named toroa-māhoe and hutihuti as the oldest.

politics.text: Kamehameha I began a military campaign in 1782 to unite the islands, and it lasted 15 years. He used western weapons and advisors such as John Young and Isaac Davis. In 1795 he conquered Oʻahu, Maui, Molokaʻi and Lānaʻi and unified them under one government. He failed to take Kauaʻi, hampered by a storm and a plague that decimated his army. In 1810 Kauaʻi and Niʻihau voluntarily joined, fully unifying the Hawaiian Islands as the Hawaiian Kingdom.

On January 17, 1893, John Good, a revolutionist, shot Leialoha, a native policeman who was trying to stop a wagon carrying weapons to the Committee of Safety. The Committee then led a coup against Queen Liliʻuokalani, kept her under armed guard, and warned that she must give up power or her subjects would face violence at the hands of the Committee and the militia. Because there was no Hawaiian army, the Committee asked American minister John L. Stevens for U.S. Marines, who never fired a shot, and the Republic of Hawaii followed in 1894. Despite claims that the overthrow was "bloodless", the Queen's Book says Mrs. J. S. Walker lost her husband through the treatment he received from the insurgents, one of many who succumbed to death from persecution.

In 1880 Pōmare V ceded Tahiti and its dependencies to France after Governor Henri Isidore Chessé, supported by the Tahitian chiefs, urged him to abdicate. Tahiti became a special colony, since all the subjects of the Kingdom of Pōmare were given French citizenship.

In 1875, Tonga's ruler Tāufaʻāhau, helped by the missionary Shirley Waldemar Baker, declared Tonga a constitutional monarchy. The new order enshrined a code of law, land tenure, and freedom of the press, giving written law and printing a place in the kingdom.

In 1875, the Tongan ruler Tāufaʻāhau, baptised Jiaoji (George) in 1831, declared Tonga a constitutional monarchy with the help of the missionary Shirley Waldemar Baker. He emancipated the serfs, enshrined a code of law, land tenure and freedom of the press, and limited the power of the chiefs.

Kauikeaouli reigned as Kamehameha III, and his rule of three decades was the longest in the monarchy's history. He enacted the Great Mahele of 1848 and promulgated the first Constitution in 1840 and its successor in 1852.

On July 6, 1844, US Secretary of State John C. Calhoun, on behalf of President Tyler, formally recognized Hawaii's independence under Kamehameha III. The kingdom then entered treaties with major nations and established over ninety legations and consulates in seaports and cities.

In 1845 the warrior and orator Tāufaʻāhau united Tonga into a more Western-style kingdom. In 1875, with help from the missionary Shirley Waldemar Baker, he declared Tonga a constitutional monarchy, emancipated the serfs, enshrined a code of law and freedom of the press, and limited the power of the chiefs.

Tāufaʻāhau was baptised with the name Jiaoji ("George") in 1831. In 1845 he united Tonga into a more Western-style kingdom. In 1875, with the help of the missionary Shirley Waldemar Baker, he declared Tonga a constitutional monarchy and emancipated the "serfs".

In 1843 Admiral Dupetit-Thouars announced the annexation of the Kingdom of Pōmare after the queen's advisor Pritchard persuaded her to display the Tahitian flag. Dupetit-Thouars threw Pritchard into prison and later sent him back to Britain. A real Franco-Tahitian war began in March 1844.

Kalākaua traveled to Washington, DC in 1874 to 1875 to gain support for a new treaty. Congress agreed to the Reciprocity Treaty of 1875 for seven years in exchange for Ford Island, and sugar farmland expanded from 12,000 acres to 125,000 acres by 1891.

The Wilcox rebellion of 1888 was a plot to overthrow King Kalākaua and replace him with his sister in a coup d'état. Princess Liliʻuokalani and Queen Kapiolani returned from Queen Victoria's Golden Jubilee immediately after news reached them in Great Britain.

On November 20, 1845, in Huahine, missionary Charles Barff gave George Seymour a letter and copies of laws and port regulations enacted by the rulers of the Leeward Islands from 1820 to 1845, affirming their independence. The next day in Raiatea, Seymour declared that Britain considered the acts establishing the French Protectorate there invalid until doubts about independence were resolved.

philosophy.text: Protestant Christian missionaries arrived in Hawaii from the United States from 1820 onwards. They eventually gained great political, moral and economic influence in the Kingdom of Hawaii, and most of the aliʻi converted to Christianity, including Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani.

Hawaiian religion was polytheistic, with many deities and spirits, and it held the animistic belief that spirits are found in animals and natural elements such as the waves and the sky. Prominent deities included Kāne, Kū, Lono and Kanaloa. Religious experts of various classes were called kahuna.

Tahiti was converted to Protestant Christianity by the London Missionary Society in the early 19th century, with the patronage of the Pōmare dynasty. Influenced by the British missionary George Pritchard, Queen Pōmare IV expelled French Catholic missionaries in 1836. This angered France and helped lead to the Franco-Tahitian War of 1844 to 1847.
In the 19th century, with the arrival of Western traders and missionaries, Tongan culture changed, especially in religion. The people discarded some old beliefs and habits and adopted others.

Samoan culture is centred on the principle of vāfealoaʻi, the relationships between people, which are based on respect, or faʻaaloalo. When Christianity was introduced, most Samoans converted. Some have subtly adapted Christianity to fit with faʻa Samoa, and ancient beliefs continue to exist alongside it.

Once the hierarchical system of religion was gone, some Hawaiians abandoned the old gods. Others kept up cultural traditions of worshipping them, especially their family ʻaumākua. After Kamehameha the Great died in 1819, Kaʻahumanu and Keōpūolani had the people burn the wooden statues and tear down the rock temples. It took Kaʻahumanu 11 years to proclaim laws against ancient religious practices, and some traditions survived through practice in hiding.

Missionaries developed a written language for the Cook Islands, bringing schools and Christianity in the early 19th century. The islands' name comes from the British navigator Captain James Cook, who arrived in the 18th century.

Ancient Hawaiian spiritual beliefs, like the lokahi, linked cultural continuity with the health of the natural world. Hawaiian scholar Mililani Trask describes a triangle with three points: the Creator, Akua; the peoples of the earth, Kanaka Maoli; and the land, the ʻaina, all in a reciprocal relationship.

culture.text: In the 1820s, the entire population of Tahiti converted to Protestantism. A visitor, Duperrey, wrote on 15 May 1823 that the missionaries of the Royal Society of London had totally changed the morals and customs of the inhabitants, and that idolatry no longer existed among them. He added that the bloody wars these people used to carry out, and their human sacrifices, had no longer taken place since 1816.

Tahiti's people celebrated the island's new place in France on 14 July 1881, amid cries of "Vive la République!" This was the first celebration of the Tiurai, the national and popular festival. It came a year after King Pōmare V ceded Tahiti to France.

Before Captain Cook's arrival, Hawaiian art included kiʻi religious images, kākau tattooing, kapa barkcloth, decorated gourds and lauhala weaving. Native Hawaiians had neither metal nor woven cloth. Production of this art continued after Cook's arrival in 1778.

Mana is a supernatural force in Melanesian and Polynesian cultures. Missionary Robert Henry Codrington published the first detailed description of it in English in his 1891 book The Melanesians. He defined it as a force distinct from physical power, acting for good and evil, and greatly advantageous to possess or control.

King David Kalākaua wrote the words of "Hawaiʻi Ponoʻī" in 1874, and the king's royal bandmaster, Captain Henri Berger, composed the music. It was adopted as the national anthem in 1876, replacing Liliʻuokalani's "He Mele Lāhui Hawaiʻi". Its melody is reminiscent of "God Save the King".

Whaling reshaped life in Hawaiian port towns. One ship arrived in Honolulu in 1820, but 110 visited in 1833. In Lahaina, 17 whaleships anchored in 1824 and 80 in 1832, with crews typically around 30 men who came to restock supplies once or twice a year.

The term Polynésie was first used in 1756 by the French writer Charles de Brosses for all the islands of the Pacific. In 1831, Jules Dumont d'Urville proposed a narrower definition in a lecture at the Société de Géographie of Paris.

In 1856, Kamehameha IV had an Anglican wedding with Emma Rooke, who was pro-British because of her British adoptive parents. Kamehameha IV established the Anglican church in Hawaii. Their only child, Prince Albert Edward Kauikeaouli Kaleiopapa a Kamehameha, died in 1862, believed to be from appendicitis, and Kamehameha IV blamed himself for the death. The couple then prioritized healthcare because diseases like leprosy and influenza were destroying the Hawaiian people.
